skill.name: Put the stages in order
skill.why: Texts are built in stages. Each stage gets the reader ready for the next.
skill.how: Ask what each part needs to come before it. Then build from the start.

steps.say: Texts are built in stages, like a tower. Bottom first! Here's Mo's recount, all jumbled up.

show.text: They got home tired but proud.
show.nudge: That wraps it all up. What do you need to know first?

show.text: Last Saturday, Gus and Mo climbed Tower Two.
Halfway up, Mo dropped the rope.
show.nudge: That's an event. Who, when and where come before it.

steps.ask: Tap the part that tells who, when and where.
steps.win: Yes! It sets things up, so it's the opening. Events come in the middle. Then the ending.

steps.say: In the middle comes what happened. Each event needs the one before. What must happen first?

show.nudge: He can't pick up a rope nobody has dropped! What comes first?
Handed back what? He needs it in his hands first.

steps.ask: Tap the event that must come first.
steps.win: Yes! Drop, pick up, hand back. Each event needs the one before it.

steps.say: Careful! All three start with a time word. Zed says that makes them all openings.

show.text: After that, Indi slid down the ice.
show.nudge: After what? 'After that' points back to something before it.

show.text: Last Friday, Indi and Zed hiked to the ice cave.
At the end, Zed said, 'Never again!'
show.nudge: That wraps up the day. It can't come first.

steps.win: Yes! It tells who, when and where, and needs nothing before it. A time word isn't enough.

steps.say: A story has stages too. First it sets the scene. Then a problem starts and grows.

show.text: Bluey the bilby lived in a sandy burrow.
show.nudge: That sets the scene. Is anything going wrong yet?

show.text: Then a flood filled the burrow with water.
Wren dug Bluey a new home on a hill.
show.nudge: That fixes things. Where does the trouble start?

steps.win: Yes! Scene, problem, solved. Some books call these orientation, complication and resolution.

steps.say: A persuasive text gives the writer's view first, then reasons. How does it end?

show.text: Firstly, fish teach us to care for animals.
show.nudge: That's a reason. It backs up the view. Find the part that sums up.

show.text: For all these reasons, please buy us a goldfish!
We believe every class needs a goldfish.
show.nudge: That gives the writer's view. It opens the letter.

steps.win: Yes! It sums up and asks the reader to act. That's how a persuasive text ends.

steps.say: A procedure opens with the goal and what you need. Then come the steps.

show.text: Pour the glue into the bowl.
show.nudge: That's a step. You can't pour glue you haven't got yet!
That's the goal itself. What do you need before the steps?

show.text: You need: glue, green paint and a bowl.

steps.ask: Tap what goes right after the goal.
steps.win: Yes! The goal, then what you need, then the steps. Each stage gets you ready for the next.

terms.means: Sets it up: who, when and where, the goal, or the writer's view.
Events, steps, reasons, or the problem. Each needs the one before.
Wraps it up: how it ended, the problem solved, or sum up and ask.

examples.text: Last Friday, Indi and Zed hiked to the ice cave.
They agreed it was the best day ever.
Fish teach us to care for animals.
So please buy us a goldfish!

card.test: What must come before this part, so it makes sense? Build up from the opening.

weDo.frame: Gus's hot chocolate steps fell down the ladder.
weDo.hint: Which step can only happen once the milk is hot?
weDo.success: You can't heat milk that isn't in the mug, or stir cocoa into milk that isn't hot yet.

items: Fill a mug with milk.
Heat the milk in the microwave for one minute.
Stir two spoons of cocoa into the hot milk.
Drop three marshmallows on top and drink it.
body.reason: Check that each step has what it needs. Is there hot milk yet to stir the cocoa into?

weDo.text: Then the wind picked up, and the rope bridge started to swing. Wren grabbed the rail and didn't let go. At last, they reached the other side, shaking but safe.
weDo.prompt: This recount is missing its opening. Which part should go first?
weDo.hint: The opening tells who, when and where. Which one does that?
weDo.success: It tells who, when and where. 'Then the wind picked up' only makes sense once they're on the bridge.

options.text: That night, they told everyone about the swinging bridge.
options.reason: 'That night' is after they crossed. It belongs at the end.

options.text: Last Sunday, Wren and Tully crossed the rope bridge to Tower Five.
Wren said she would never cross a rope bridge again.
options.reason: She can only say 'never again' after the crossing. This belongs at the end.

creature.name: Stagglet
creature.blurb: A silver alpine butterfly that grows in stages: egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, then wings. It can't skip a stage, and neither can a text.

write.ask: Write the opening for this recount. Tell who, when and where.
given: We waded into the freezing water.
checks: My opening tells who was there
It makes sense with nothing before it
write.model: Last Sunday, Gus and I went to the rock pools at Gull Bay.

encounters.frame: Mo's snow cone recipe fell down the ladder. A Stagglet is sitting on the jumbled cards.
encounters.prompt: Put Mo's steps in order.
encounters.success: Snow in, press it, pour on cordial, eat. Each step uses what the step before made.

items: Scoop some snow into a paper cup.
Press the snow down hard with a spoon.
Pour the cordial over the pressed snow.
Eat it quickly, before it all melts.
body.reason: Each step needs the one before. You can't press snow that isn't in the cup yet.

encounters.frame: Tully wrote a recount of Saturday's game. The Stagglet shuffled the pages.
encounters.prompt: Put Tully's recount in order.
encounters.success: Who, when and where come first. The lost ball, the spare ball and the goal follow, then what happened after.

items: On Saturday, Tully's team played footy in the snow.
In the first quarter, Tully kicked the ball into a snowdrift.
Nobody could find it, so the umpire got out a spare ball.
With the spare ball, Tully kicked the winning goal.
After the game, they found the first ball frozen in the drift.
body.reason: The umpire only needs a spare ball once the first one is lost. Find what each part needs.

encounters.frame: The Stagglet's cousin is a Bogong moth. Someone moved a line in its life story.
encounters.prompt: One sentence has been moved to the wrong place. Tap it.
encounters.success: There's no moth yet at that point, only an egg. Flying to the mountains belongs at the very end.

parts.tap: A Bogong moth starts life as a tiny egg on a leaf.
parts.reason: This is the very start of its life, so it belongs first.

parts.tap: The new moth flies all the way to the mountains.
The egg hatches into a hungry caterpillar.
parts.reason: This comes right after the egg. It's in the right place.

parts: The caterpillar eats leaves all winter and grows fat.

parts.tap: Then it digs into the soil and makes a hard case around itself.
parts.reason: It digs in after it has grown fat. This is in the right place.

parts.tap: In spring, a moth crawls out of the case.
parts.reason: The moth can only crawl out after the case is made. This fits.

parts: It dries its wings in the warm sun.

encounters.frame: The Stagglet found half a story in the Tower Six hut. The next page is missing.
encounters.text: Bea lived in a little hut at the foot of Tower Six. One night, a storm howled around the hut. Bea was tucked up in bed when she heard a noise. Scratch. Scratch. Scratch. It was coming from the roof! She grabbed her torch and crept outside into the wind. Something small was stuck in the gutter. It was squeaking.
encounters.prompt: Which part should come next?
encounters.success: Bea has just found something in the gutter. Next she has to get it out and see what it is.

options.text: Once upon a time, a girl called Bea lived in a hut.
options.reason: That's an opening. We already know who Bea is and where she lives.

options.text: So Bea put the possum back in the gutter.
options.reason: She can't put it back before she lifts it out. And we don't know it's a possum yet.

options.text: Bea reached up and lifted it out. It was a baby possum.

encounters.frame: Indi wrote a procedure for painting a snow gum. The Stagglet chewed it into pieces.
encounters.prompt: Match each piece to its stage of the procedure.
encounters.success: The goal names what you'll make. Then comes what you need. The steps tell you what to do.

items.text: How to Paint a Snow Gum
items.reason: This names what you will make. That's the goal, at the top.

items.text: a big sheet of paper
items.reason: This is a thing to get ready before you start.

items.text: Paint a twisty grey trunk.
items.reason: This tells you what to do. It's a step.

items.text: three pots of paint
items.reason: This is a thing you need before you start.

items.text: a thin brush
items.reason: This is a tool you need before you start.

items.text: Add red and yellow stripes to the bark.
items.reason: This tells you what to do to the trunk. It's a step.

encounters.frame: Indi drew a comic of Mo's worst day. The Stagglet mixed up the panels.
encounters.text: Mo was the worst cook on Scaffold Peaks. But he was very proud of his pies. One morning, he baked a giant meat pie for the Peaks Picnic. The pie was still hot, and it smelled amazing. The picnic was at the very top of Tower Two. That meant fifty rungs of ladder, with a pie in one hand. What could possibly go wrong?
encounters.prompt: Here's how Mo's story starts. Put the rest in order.
encounters.success: The pie slips, lands on the goat, gets eaten, and only then does Mo need a new one.

items: Halfway up the ladder, the pie slipped out of Mo's hand.
It spun through the air and landed on a goat's head.
The goat licked its lips and ate the whole pie.
So Mo climbed down and baked another pie. This time, he used a backpack.
body.reason: The goat can't eat the pie until it lands on its head. Find what each part needs.

encounters.frame: Gus grazed his knee on Tower Three. He's explaining his scab to anyone who will listen.
encounters.prompt: Put Gus's explanation of a scab in order.
encounters.success: Broken tubes, leaking blood, a net of platelets, a crusty scab, then new skin. Each step causes the next.

items: When you graze your knee, tiny blood tubes under the skin break open.
Blood leaks out, and sticky cells called platelets rush to the graze.
The platelets clump together and spin a net of threads that traps the blood.
The trapped blood dries out and hardens into a crusty brown scab.
Under the scab, new skin grows, until one day the scab falls off by itself.
body.reason: Each step causes the next. Blood can't be trapped until the platelets have made their net.

encounters.frame: Gus is teaching the Stagglet to build a tiny buzzing robot. The steps got shuffled.
encounters.prompt: Put the steps for building a bristlebot in order.
encounters.success: Each step builds on the one before: head, tape, motor, battery, then the buzz that makes it scuttle.

items: Snip the bristly head off an old toothbrush.
Stick a strip of foam tape on top of the snipped-off head.
Press a tiny buzzing motor onto the foam tape.
Tape a flat coin battery beside the motor.
Touch the motor's loose wire to the battery, and the motor starts to buzz.
Set your buzzing bot on the table and watch it scuttle away.
body.reason: Check what each step needs. The battery goes beside the motor, so the motor must be on first.

encounters.frame: Tully's ski race recount is pinned up in the Tower One hut. Someone has moved a part.
encounters.prompt: One part of Tully's recount has been moved. Tap it.
encounters.success: She can't get a medal at the bottom before the race has even started. That part belongs after the finish.

parts: Last Sunday, Tully entered her very first ski race, on the steep north slope of Mount Ladder.

parts.tap: Before the start, she waxed her skis and checked her boot buckles twice.
parts.reason: Getting ready comes before the race starts. This is in the right place.

parts.tap: At the bottom, the judges hung a silver medal around her neck.

parts: At the starting gate, her knees were wobbling, and she could hear her heart thumping.

parts.tap: When the horn blew, she pushed off and flew down the slope.
parts.reason: This is the start of the race, right after the gate. It fits.

parts.tap: Halfway down, she skidded on a patch of ice but kept her balance.
parts.reason: Halfway down comes after she pushes off. It fits.

parts.tap: She crossed the finish line in second place, just behind a Year 6 boy.
parts.reason: Finishing comes after the middle of the run. It fits.

parts: That night, she slept with the medal still on, and she snored like a snowplough.

encounters.frame: The Stagglet is reading an explanation in the telescope tower. A sentence has fallen out.
encounters.text: How the Moon Seems to Change Shape. The Moon does not make any light of its own. ___ As the Moon travels around Earth, we see different amounts of that sunlit half. When we can see all of the sunlit half, we call it a full Moon. When we can see only half of it, we call it a half Moon. When we can see just a thin sliver, we call it a crescent. It takes about a month for the Moon to go all the way around Earth and start again. That is why the Moon seems to change shape through the month, even though it is always round.
encounters.prompt: Which sentence fills the gap?
encounters.success: The next sentence talks about 'that sunlit half'. So the gap must first say the Sun lights up one half.

options.text: Instead, the Sun shines on it and lights up one half.
When we can see none of the sunlit half, we call it a new Moon.
options.reason: This talks about 'the sunlit half' before the text has said what lights the Moon.

options.text: So the Moon stays dark, and nobody on Earth can see it.
options.reason: That doesn't fit. The very next sentence says we see its sunlit half.

encounters.frame: The Stagglet is helping Wren sort her recount of the band concert into stages.
encounters.prompt: Match each sentence to its stage of the recount.
encounters.success: The opening sets up who, when and where. The events go in order. The ending wraps up the night.

items.text: Last Friday night, the Peakside band played at the Snow Gum Hall.
items.reason: This tells who, when and where. It sets up the recount.

items.text: First, the drummer counted us in, and we started our first song.
items.reason: This is the first event of the concert.

items.text: Halfway through, a string on Maya's violin snapped, but she borrowed Mr Lin's and kept going.
items.reason: This happened in the middle of the concert. The snap and the borrowed violin are both events.

items.text: After that, Gus sang a slow song in a very wobbly voice.
items.reason: This is the next event, after Maya's violin trouble. The concert isn't over yet.

items.text: At the end, the crowd cheered, and we went home tired but proud.
items.reason: This wraps up the night: the cheering, going home and how they felt.

encounters.frame: Mo is telling the Stagglet a story about a pelican. He keeps losing his place.
encounters.prompt: Put Mo's story in order.
encounters.success: The note comes in the bottle, so Ari rows out, meets the pelican, then brings it home.

items: One windy morning, Ari found a glass bottle bobbing in Gull Bay, with a note inside.
The note said, 'Help! I'm stuck on Gull Rock. Please bring chips.'
Ari rowed her little boat out to Gull Rock as fast as she could.
When she got there, a very grumpy pelican was sitting on the rock, holding a pen in its beak.
Ari shared her chips and rowed the pelican back to shore, and it never wrote another note.
body.reason: Ari can't read the note before she finds the bottle. Look for what each part needs first.

encounters.frame: Mo is making damper on the campfire at Base Camp. The Stagglet thinks his recipe card is muddled.
encounters.prompt: One stage of Mo's recipe is in the wrong place. Which one?
encounters.success: What you need comes before the steps. By step 1, the cook is already using the flour.

options.text: the title, 'Campfire Damper'
options.reason: The goal comes first, so the title is already in the right place.

options.text: the list of what you need
the tip about eating it warm
options.reason: A tip like this can wrap up a procedure, after the steps are done.

options.text: the warning to ask an adult
options.reason: A safety note belongs near the start, before anyone goes near the coals.

encounters.text: Campfire Damper. Damper is a simple bush bread that you cook in the coals of a campfire. Ask an adult to help, because the coals are very hot. Step 1: Rub the flour, salt and butter together until it looks like breadcrumbs. Step 2: Pour in the milk and stir until it turns into a soft dough. You will need: two cups of self-raising flour, a pinch of salt, a knob of butter, one cup of milk and a sheet of foil. Step 3: Shape the dough into a round loaf and wrap it in the foil. Step 4: Bury it in the hot coals for thirty minutes, then dig it out. Your damper is cooked if it sounds hollow when you tap the bottom. Eat it warm with golden syrup, and save a piece for the Stagglet.

encounters.frame: Zed wrote a story about the Peaks Gaming Cup. The Stagglet is hunting for where the trouble starts.
encounters.prompt: Tap the sentence where the problem in Zed's story starts.
encounters.success: The missing controller is the problem. Before it, Zed's lucky wins only set the scene.

parts.tap: Zed had won the Peaks Gaming Cup three years in a row, always with his lucky blue controller.
parts.reason: This sets the scene: who Zed is and what he's proud of. Nothing has gone wrong yet.

parts.tap: On the morning of this year's final, he opened his bag and froze, because the controller wasn't there.
He searched the hut, the ladder and the snow outside, but it was nowhere to be found.
parts.reason: This makes a problem worse. What went wrong just before it?

parts: With ten minutes to go, he had to borrow a sticky old controller from the lost-property box.

parts.tap: Every jump came out late, and by the last level he had dropped to fourth place.
parts.reason: The problem is at its worst here, but it started earlier.

parts.tap: Then he remembered something Gus always said about old controllers: press early, because their buttons are slow.
parts.reason: This is where the problem starts to be solved.

parts: He pressed every jump a moment early, and he flew past the other three players to win. That night, he found the blue controller in the fridge, right next to Mo's custard.

encounters.frame: Mo copied out Indi's painting procedure for the Stagglet, but he left out a step.
encounters.text: How to Paint a Night Sky over the Peaks. This painting looks best on thick paper, because thin paper wrinkles when it gets wet. Ask an adult to cover the table with newspaper first. You will need a pencil, one wide brush, a jar of water and three paints: dark blue, white and black. 1. Sketch the outline of the rock towers lightly in pencil, along the bottom of the page. 2. Paint the whole sky dark blue, right up to the pencil line. 3. Dip the same brush in white paint and dab stars across the wet sky, so they blur a little and glow. 4. Fill in the rock towers with black paint, then leave the whole picture to dry flat overnight. Your painting should be dry and ready to hang by breakfast. If it curls at the edges, press it flat under a pile of heavy books for a day.
encounters.prompt: Mo left out this step: 'Rinse the blue off your brush in the jar of water.' Where does it belong?
encounters.success: The blue gets on the brush in step 2. It must come off before step 3 dips it in white.

options.text: between steps 1 and 2
options.reason: The brush hasn't touched any paint yet, so there's no blue to rinse off.

options.text: between steps 3 and 4
options.reason: By step 3 the brush is already in the white. The blue has to come off first.

options.text: between steps 2 and 3
after step 4
options.reason: That's far too late. The white stars would already be streaky blue.

encounters.frame: Wren's rescue diary got wet, and the Stagglet is trying to put the pages back in order.
encounters.prompt: Put Wren's recount in order, from the opening to the ending.
encounters.success: Opening, events, then an ending that looks back. The last part has no time word, but it wraps up.

items: On Tuesday morning, Wren found a crimson rosella in the snow beside Tower Two.
She carried it down to the hut and found that one wing was bruised.
For a week, she fed it seeds and slices of apple in a warm box.
On the next Tuesday, she watched it fly off to join its noisy flock.
Wren still looks up at every rosella, hoping it might be hers.
body.reason: Which part looks back on everything that happened? It needs every event before it.

encounters.frame: Room 3 wrote a persuasive letter about robot helpers. The Stagglet is sorting the pieces.
encounters.prompt: Match each part of the letter to its stage.
encounters.success: The opening gives the writer's view. Each reason backs it up. The ending sums up and asks for action.

items.text: Imagine a classroom where a robot hands out the pencils. We believe every classroom should have one.
items.reason: 'Imagine' draws you in, and 'We believe' states the view the letter will argue.

items.text: Firstly, robots never get tired, so they could help with jobs all day long.
items.reason: This gives one reason to back up the view.

items.text: Secondly, a robot helper would give teachers more time to help students.
items.reason: This gives a second reason to back up the view.

items.text: Finally, building and fixing the robot would teach us real engineering skills.
items.reason: 'Finally' starts the last reason, but it's still a reason, not the ending.

items.text: For all these reasons, our school must get a robot helper. Please sign our letter to the principal.
items.reason: 'For all these reasons' sums up, and 'Please sign' asks the reader to act.

encounters.frame: Tully is telling a scary story around the campfire. The Stagglet keeps interrupting, so it's jumbled.
encounters.prompt: Put Tully's story in order, from the scene to the end.
encounters.success: 'At last' sounds like an ending, but it's just the crew arriving. Scene, problem, then the goat solves it.

items: The old weather station on Tower Six had been empty for fifty years.
At last, after a long climb, the crew reached its door and found it hanging open.
Inside, every clock had stopped at midnight, and something was thumping in the cellar.
Gus crept down the cellar stairs and flung the door open.
A very old goat wandered out, chewing a weather report, and the crew laughed until they cried.
body.reason: 'At last' tells when they arrived, not that the story is over. What must come before 'Inside'?

encounters.frame: Ari wrote a recount for the class blog. The Stagglet is reading the last line twice.
encounters.prompt: Why did Ari end with 'That was the day the ocean stopped being scary' instead of one more event?
encounters.success: It's the recount's ending stage. It looks back on the whole day and tells the reader what it meant.

options.text: It looks back on the day and says what it meant to Ari.
It tells the last thing Ari did before she fell asleep.
options.reason: Falling asleep was the last event. Nothing new happens in this line.

options.text: It shows that Ari's problem has not been solved yet.
options.reason: Her fear is solved. The ocean has stopped being scary.

options.text: It hints that Ari will write about her next snorkelling trip with Mum soon.
options.reason: Nothing points to another trip. Ari is thinking about this day.

encounters.text: Last Saturday, Mum took me snorkelling at Gull Bay for the very first time. I had never put my face under the sea before, and my stomach was in knots. First, Mum showed me how to spit in my mask so it wouldn't fog up, which was disgusting but worked. Then we waded in up to our waists, and I practised breathing through the snorkel while standing still. When I finally put my face in, I forgot to breathe at all, because a school of silver fish was flashing past my knees. Mum tapped my shoulder and pointed at a rock covered in purple sea urchins. Near the jetty, a huge blue groper swam right up to my mask and stared at me as if I was the strange one. By the time we came out, my fingers were wrinkly and my lips were salty, and I didn't want to leave. On the drive home, I fell asleep with my mask still on my head. That was the day the ocean stopped being scary and started being mine.

encounters.frame: Room 6's persuasive text is going to the council. The Stagglet ate the last page.
encounters.text: Build a Climbing Wall at Peaks Park! Every winter, Peaks Park sits empty, because there is nothing for young people to do there once the snow arrives. Our class believes the council should turn the old boat shed into an indoor climbing wall, and there are three strong reasons. Firstly, climbing builds strength, balance and confidence, and it is a sport that people of any size or age can enjoy. Doctors say that children who climb often sleep better and find it easier to concentrate at school. Unlike footy or netball, you don't need a whole team, so you can climb whenever you have a spare hour. Secondly, the nearest climbing gym is a two-hour bus ride away, which means most families on the island never get the chance to try it. A wall in the park would put the sport within walking distance of every school on Scaffold Peaks. Thirdly, a climbing wall would bring visitors to the park all year round, even in the middle of a blizzard. Those visitors would spend money in the local cafes and shops, which struggle every winter when the tourists stay away. The park's kiosk, which closes every June, could even stay open and hire local teenagers.
encounters.prompt: This persuasive text is missing its final stage. Which part should come last?
encounters.success: A persuasive text ends by summing up its view and asking the reader to act. Only this part does both.

options.text: A fourth reason is that climbing walls also help people get over their fear of heights, which matters on an island of ladders.
options.reason: The text promised three reasons and gave all three. Another reason doesn't sum up or ask for anything.

options.text: Peaks Park is a large, grassy area beside the harbour, with a playground, a boat shed and a small car park.
options.reason: This describes the park. It's background for the start, not an ending.

options.text: For all these reasons, the council should build the wall before next winter. Please sign our petition at the library.
Last year, my cousin tried climbing in the city, and she loved it so much that she went back every weekend.
options.reason: This is a small story. It doesn't sum up the reasons or ask the reader to do anything.

encounters.frame: An astronaut's diary has floated down to Scaffold Peaks. The Stagglet thinks a page was put back wrong.
encounters.prompt: One stage of the astronaut's recount has been moved. Tap it.
encounters.success: That sentence tells who, when and where. It's the opening, so it belongs before every event.

parts.tap: The preparation began at dawn, when Sasha helped me squeeze into the bulky white suit and checked every seal twice.
parts.reason: This is the first event. Something should set it up, but the event itself is in order.

parts.tap: Next, we spent an hour in the airlock breathing pure oxygen, so that our bodies would be ready for the low pressure outside.
parts.reason: This event follows getting suited up, so it's in the right place.

parts.tap: My name is Ayana Okoye, and yesterday I made my first spacewalk, six hours outside the space station.
When the outer hatch finally swung open, Earth filled the whole doorway, blue and impossibly bright.
parts.reason: The hatch opens after the airlock, so this event is in order.

parts: For a few seconds I forgot to move at all, until Sasha's voice crackled in my helmet. I clipped my safety line to the rail and pulled myself, hand over hand, towards the broken solar panel. A speck of space dust had cracked it right across the middle. Replacing it took almost four hours, because every bolt had to be loosened with thick, clumsy gloves.

parts.tap: By the time we floated back into the airlock, my fingers ached and my stomach was rumbling.
parts.reason: 'By the time' sounds like an ending, but this is still an event, after the repair.

parts: Afterwards, the crew had saved me a pouch of warm spaghetti, which I ate upside down. Now my arms feel like that spaghetti, but I would go out again tomorrow.

encounters.frame: Mo is telling the Stagglet about the Bake-Off, but he's too excited to tell it in order.
encounters.prompt: Put Mo's Bake-Off story in order, from the scene to the end.
encounters.success: Scene, problem, worse, solved, then a look back. 'Finally' is a time word, not the ending stage.

items: Mo was the proudest baker on Scaffold Peaks, and the Bake-Off was his big day.
Halfway through mixing, he tipped in two cups of salt instead of sugar.
Finally, the judges reached his salty cake, took one bite and spat it out.
So Mo baked a tiny new sponge in twenty minutes flat, and this time the judges loved it.
He still keeps his Best Comeback ribbon stuck to the fridge.
body.reason: 'Finally' tells when the judges tasted it, not that the story is over. What fixes the problem?

encounters.frame: Gus made a plan of the stages in the band's recount. The Stagglet thinks he got the ending wrong.
encounters.text: Last Saturday, the Peakside Primary band played its biggest concert yet, at the Snow Gum Hall on top of Tower Five. We arrived at four o'clock, lugging our instruments up the last ladder, and spent an hour on a sound check while Mr Lin fussed over the microphones. The hall filled up quickly, and by seven every seat was taken. Even the Architect had come, sitting in the front row with a notebook open. Our first three songs went perfectly, and the audience clapped along to the fourth. Then, halfway through our fifth song, a storm knocked out the power, and the whole hall went black. For a moment, nobody moved. Somebody's baby started to cry, and somebody's grandad woke up with a snort. Then Tully switched on the torch on her phone, and one by one the audience did the same, until the stage was lit by hundreds of tiny lights. We played the rest of the concert by torchlight, without microphones, and somehow it sounded even better. When we finished our final song, the crowd begged for more, so we played it all again as an encore. The power came back on just as we were packing up, which everyone agreed was perfect timing.

encounters.success: The encore is the last song, but the recount ends after it: the power comes back on during packing up.

encounters.frame: Indi is planning a picture book about a possum on Scaffold Peaks. The Stagglet is helping her sort the stages.
encounters.prompt: Match each sentence to its stage in the story.
encounters.success: The first two set the scene. The builders start the trouble and the truck makes it worse. Wren solves it.

items.text: High on Tower Six, in a hut that nobody had used for years, lived a mountain pygmy possum called Pinch.
items.reason: This introduces who and where. Nothing has gone wrong yet.

items.text: Every autumn, Pinch filled the hut's old teapot with seeds, ready for her long winter sleep.
items.reason: This shows Pinch's normal life before the trouble starts.

items.text: Then one morning, a terrible crash woke Pinch: builders were smashing the hut's walls to make room for Maxx World.
items.reason: The crash and the smashed walls are trouble. Pinch's normal life is over, so the problem has begun.

items.text: By lunchtime, the builders had carried off the teapot, seeds and all, and tossed it onto a truck.
items.reason: Losing her winter food makes Pinch's problem worse.

items.text: As the truck rumbled away and the first snow began to fall, Pinch had nowhere to sleep and nothing to eat.
items.reason: This is the problem at its worst: winter is coming and everything is gone.

items.text: Wren chased the truck to the bottom of the hill, rescued the teapot, then found Pinch and tucked them both into a hollow log.
items.reason: Wren fixes everything: Pinch gets her seeds back and a new home.
